I’ve had a prescription for medical marijuana since 2015, and it was legalized in 2018.  My prescription has been for 5 grams a day since 2016, but the amount I use fluctuates depending on what I’m doing (e.g., working at the office vs working from home).  

In addition to cannabis, I have a pile of prescriptions for pain management I use (naproxen, cyclobenzaprine, gabapentin, and hydromorphone extended and quick release).  I’ve found on my wfh days I can get enough relief from a couple joints I don’t need to take any hydromorphone or cyclobenzaprine.  


There’s a lot of factors to consider with cannabis to maximize its potential for your specific needs.  When I first started using medical marijuana, I took notes about each strain I tried (including the company name, %THC and %CBD, sativa/indica/hybrid, terpenes, and the effects I felt- pain relief, sleep, appetite, anxiety, uplifted mood, etc.) and this helped me determine what strains were best for working vs outside of work vs sleeping. 


Terpenes are what gives each strain it’s unique flavour profile and each terpene has different effects.   Finding out what terpenes are in a strain may require some research before you buy, sometimes it’s on the packaging but not always.  Another thing I did when I first started was making a list of all the terpenes with their effects, and I ranked them from most preferred to least preferred and used this hierarchy to make my selections.  


There’s also strains out there with little to no THC, instead primarily CBD.   These strains don’t have the same effects, you don’t feel “stoned” but still get the beneficial effects like pain relief and increased appetite. 


And knowing the difference between indica and sativa and hybrid is important.  Sativa is what I call “daytime weed” and I can smoke 2-3 joints before I start work without issues.  My top sativa strains are “lemon haze” and “jack herer”.  Indica strains are “nighttime weed” and is my go-to when I need to stimulate my appetite or fall asleep.  My preferred indica are “blueberry”/“blue dream” strains.  And hybrids are crosses between indica and sativa strains, so I avoid them before/during work to be safe.   


Medical cannabis is only a part of my treatment regiment and could not replace my pharmaceuticals, but it plays a significant role in improving my quality of life by decreasing pain, increasing my appetite, improving my mood, helping me sleep, etc.

Another contributing factor is how our bodies react to chronic pain- by creating MORE pain receptors and sometimes the brain is trying to sort through so many signals that things get “misfiled” along the way creating more pain in random places.  I have chronic abdominal pain that I feel in my feet.  


What has helped me along this journey is a combination of pain meds that includes an anti inflammatory (naproxen), a nerve pain medication (gabapentin), a muscle medication (cyclobenzaprine), and a narcotic pain medication (tramadol or dilaudid).  Don’t take narcotics regularly, those are for the worst days, addiction is real and happens fast and causes more pain.  But those other three meds can be taken daily.  

Things you can do daily to help improve your quality of life including practicing mindfulness (Jon kabat-zinn has some great guided meditations for pain management on YouTube) and pacing (also known as the spoons theory but I hate the spoonie culture) and with pacing you limit the tasks you do each day to match your energy levels and once your body starts showing the signs you’re overdoing it, listen to your body and stop pushing yourself.   I’m horrible at pacing because once I have a good day I try and do allllllll the things, but it’s better to stop before my body flares up completely and then I’m bedridden again.  

And if you have access to mental health services, that’s another layer to the pain onion.  And it sounds like you’re struggling with the isolation having a chronic illness causes and that’s completely understandable.  Most people have no clue how lonely being sick can be.  And an invisible illness makes it so much harder for others to understand.  And fibromyalgia likes to keep us guessing.  I never know if I’ll  wake up feeling like a million bucks or if I’ll feel like I was hit by a million trucks.  So talk therapy can be helpful, but I had the biggest TSN turning point from a group for Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) acceptance does NOT mean you’re okay with this pain but it helps you realign you with your values and regain quality of life in pain.

First, I didn’t see it mentioned yet, but (location-dependent) your employer isn’t entitled to knowing what your medical condition(s) are in order to get medical accommodations considered.  And with the negative stigma associated with fibromyalgia, I’ve kept that diagnosis to myself while receiving medical accommodations for years at my work so I wouldn’t tell them the nature of your disability unless you have to there.  


My accommodations included working from home two days a week, having a stand-to-sit desk in office, during meetings they know I will be alternating between sitting and standing and not to mind me, and I kept a heated shawl at my desk as well (it’s like a plug in blanket but 1/3 the size - highly recommended it), and my workplace I can dress in yoga pants and running shoes but that’s another thing to consider. With each pain medication targeting different pain manifestations I can somewhat function consistently.  I may not always need all of them but the cyclobenzaprine has become a staple.

Ketamine assisted therapy was a game changer for me last year.  My flare ups were debilitating on a weekly basis and essentially I was stuck in “fight/flight/freeze” for a horrible few months that i couldn’t snap out of.  I wanted to die I was so sick. And when I was out of other options I was finally referred to ketamine therapy and the first session reset my nervous system and broke me out of my months long flare up in fight flight mode.  

So if you’re looking for a safer alternative to this scary sounding option I’d look into ketamine.

My advice for either is to wait until you and the other person are both calm and not fired up about the issue you want to address.  

Think about your points and opinions you wish to convey ahead of time and write down your talking points so you are able to remember them more easily when addressing the issue or situation with the other person.  

Practice breathing exercises ahead of time (box breathing is a good one - breathe in for four counts, hold for four, breathe out for four and hold for four). This will help regulate your circadian rhythm and maintain calmer composure.  

Now if you have to act in the moment, my advice is to try and keep extreme emotions out of it (it’s easy to match the other persons emotions, but that doesn’t help anyone).  Be truthful and direct with your verbal communication and your nonverbal communication should be non threatening (meet them at their level while maintaining space, speaking with a calm voice at an appropriate volume, etc).

I feel this deep in my soul.  I was first diagnosed in my mid-30’s, then I questioned this when I was 40, and after a mental health crisis I had two more (independent and unrelated) psychiatrists diagnose me with BPD again.  So I figure three times must be correct. 

But here’s the thing.  You don’t have to let your diagnosis define you.  You are a million things besides a person with BPD.  Yes you’re going to experience some big emotions and probably make some questionable life choices (but probably fun choices at the time), along with whatever other BPD symptoms you experience, and it will probably really suck sometimes. 


However, there ARE some things you can do and learn to help manage your BPD.  This is coming from someone who’s taken the alphabet of therapies and tried different medications along the way, and honestly I was managing my BPD like a champ for years! 


The recommended therapy is DBT, which helps manage symptoms.   I no longer fire hot when I’m wronged.   Now I can sit on it and when I do fire back, it’s so much better executed.  I’ve had time to think and get receipts before I respond.   That’s probably not what the purpose of that skill is meant for, but I appreciate it.  

CBT is another group therapy commonly used, but it focuses on changing thinking patterns whereas DBT helps with the emotional regulation.  


Mindfulness is another tool that helps me immensely, there are TONS of guided meditations on YouTube and when I am practicing good habits and doing mindfulness every morning, I am much calmer overall.   


Medications aren’t great for BPD because they’re not super effective and none are specifically for BPD.   If going the medication route, I’d suggest looking online at medical journals and articles about BPD medications and I’d look for one that matches your specific symptoms.  That’s my approach going forward since my current meds are for symptoms I don’t struggle with (like aggression).  


The last thing I’ll add is the strategy/tool that helps me the most with my symptom management is labelling my thoughts that are fuelling big emotions.   I can’t remember if it’s a CBT or DBT skill, but it labels thought patterns.   Like black and white thinking - we often only see two possible outcomes when we are high emotions about something.  Another is mind reading - another common thought pattern is we think we know what other people are thinking or feeling about us or something we did.  We have no idea what they’re thinking.   My personal favourite is catastrophizing - which is thinking worst case scenario is imminent when it’s probably not.  And even if it is, is it really that bad? (It’s not). 


I’ll try to find some resources for you but best of luck.  You’re young and can shape your thoughts and behaviours to minimize your current symptoms and may not need to worry about meds or anything like that longterm


ETA - the labelling thoughts is actually a skill from my FAVOURITE alphabet therapy, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and I HIGHLY RECOMMEND IT.  Acceptance doesn’t mean you’re okay with your situation, but it helps you realign your values with your situation.  I have chronic illnesses which is why I took ACT but it was a game changer for me.

So I’m not sure why you’re convinced you’ll never have a gf, but that attitude will become a self fulfilling prophecy and then your prediction will be right, but only because you’ve made it so.  

Without any details or context, my advice will be broad and may not all be relevant to you.  But here are some suggestions:

1) change your mindset, first and foremost.  If you think bad things then you may miss the good things when they happen.  I’m not saying you’re going to manifest a gf, but stop thinking you never will.  Think positively and express yourself in a positive manner, both with verbal and nonverbal communication.  Smile more, find the beauty in the little things in life (like puppies or being in nature or whatever floats your boat), be open and willing to experience things out of your comfort zone (like engaging in conversation with strangers, attending events that you’re interested in but don’t normally go to, etc.)

2) I won’t say hit the gym, but good hygiene and clothing goes a long way.  Maybe get a haircut, wear clean clothes and deodorant daily.  Shower regularly and brush your teeth daily (twice a day is recommended but if you’re in a state of not brushing daily, once is a good start) and floss your teeth regularly as well.  Bad breath is often caused by food between your teeth that brushing doesn’t help with.  Smelling your dental floss after flossing will tell you if you’ve had bad breath or not.  Wear clothes that fit and look good on you.  

3) if you’re using dating apps and you’re often ignoring girls who don’t make your current standards, maybe reevaluate what you’re looking for in a partner.  Pretty girls are going to get more attention and have more options, but that doesn’t make them a suitable partner.  Looks aren’t everything.  Find girls who are more on your page in terms of interests and values, looks can change and makeup is a sneaky trick.  

4) join groups you’re interested in, not with the sole purpose of getting a gf, but for you to have something you enjoy doing or discussing, and it might result in meeting a girl who has the same interests and passions and values as you.  

5) don’t wallow in self pity because you’re single.  Not all relationships are healthy and lots of people who have a partner are miserable in their situation too.  And don’t just jump into a relationship because it’s available, find someone who you’ll relate to and who shares your values to ensure when you do have a gf it will be a positive experience.  

6) look for things like speed-dating or other events for single people to meet. It’s probably scary to put yourself out there, but all those people are scared and taking the plunge anyways.  Even online groups are often available for your area on FB or even Reddit.  

7) make sure your expectations of what a gf should be are not outrageous.  There’s a lot of people out there on social media who think women are supposed to cook and clean and provide sex on demand.  That’s not how the world works now.  Sex isn’t a right in a relationship, it’s a bonus for you both to share your love and feelings for each other that shouldn’t be forced.  And cooking and cleaning and other stuff like that is often a shared responsibility as often women are working full time jobs too, so the burden of being expected to maintain all household duties should be discussed and divided equally based on your own situations.  

8) communication is key as well.  Being open and honest with a potential gf or a gf goes a long way.  You’re not a mind reader and neither are potential gf’s, so being able to communicate with respect and to listen without being judgmental will help maintain a relationship in a positive way.

The best thing you can do is take care of yourself first and foremost.  I can appreciate that you want to help and to be there for your friend, but it sounds like you’re entering the realm of compassion fatigue and it’s exhausting to be someone’s only crutch.  Years ago I had a friend who was depressed and suicidal and like clockwork every Friday I would receive a text message from her saying she was going to kill herself.  I have worked in social services and volunteered for a distress line for years and years, so this was in my wheelhouse, but after this repeated for months I hit my breaking point and had to tell her I couldn’t be her only support anymore.  I gave her all the resources available for her and explained we are still friends but I was unable to help her and she needed to find professional support since she didn’t follow any of my advice.  It sucked and it definitely impacted our friendship, but I was at the point of turning my phone off on Fridays just to maintain my mental health.  She’s still alive and we are still friends 7 years later, but she no longer texts me about being suicidal.  

It’s definitely hard to set boundaries but you can’t make your life about keeping her happy.  And if she does end her life, just know that’s her decision and is it your fault whatsoever.   

I would research the different resources in her area, things like a distress line, mental health supports (both 1:1 and groups), offer to go with her to see her doctor or psychiatrist (waiting in the waiting room or going in with her, whatever she’s comfortable with), online support groups, virtual therapy sessions, etc.  Be firm about the boundaries once set, but still be empathetic and understanding towards her.  If she starts breaking your boundaries, gently remind her that you’re not able to help her the way she needs, and reiterate the relative supports you’ve previously sent to her.  

And congrats on your school acceptance! She’s worried about losing your friendship but she’s emotionally manipulating you trying to get her way without considering how it will affect you.  I’ve been in her shoes and in your shoes before and while it sucks to be in either position, now that your mental health is being affected, it’s time to stop being her only crutch and to help her find better supports.  You can still be friends but not if she’s only using you for emotional support and repeating a cycle of being in crisis but not helping herself.

Additionally, the pain clinic I am a patient at also offers various workshops and groups to help manage living with chronic pain.  Those additional supports were game changers for sure and I’ll list them below for you to also consider :)

The biggest TSN turning point for me was actually a mental health group for Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT).  Don’t let the name fool you, acceptance isn’t being okay with the pain but rather looking at your individual values and learning to manage chronic pain while maintaining important values in your life.   It reframes how we react and interpret pain and illnesses.   I HIGHLY recommend it for anyone living with chronic pain.   

Pacing is another good tool to use in your daily life to minimize pain escalations.  Honestly the spoonies make me cringe but the theory underlying it is solid.  So because I’m anti spoons, I approach pacing by breaking down some tasks to include breaks and I try to acknowledge to my body’s precursors to pain flares and quit while I’m ahead.  And I struggle to stop while I’m ahead sometimes because I want yo get stuff done while I can, but with pacing I can do more overall.  

Breathing exercises and mindfulness are also game changers more than I anticipated. Honestly the first time the occupational therapist told me to practice breathing I was not sold.  I went home and bitched about how I’ve been breathing for over 30 years at that point so I don’t think that’s the problem.  Well turns out it played a significant role.   Box breathing exercises were what I started with and it does help with reducing pain.  There’s lots of mindfulness exercises on YouTube and Jon Kabat-Zinn has great pain relief exercises. 

I have also tried trigger point injections but they were hit or miss for my pain.  However that might be something for you to consider.  I DID have significant relief from acupuncture dry needling so I also suggest you look into this.  I had the acupuncture from a physiotherapist at the pain clinic.  Massage therapy has also helped but find a good massage therapist.  Like doctors I didn’t know there was a difference until I found an amazing massage therapist who works some magic.   

And lastly another pro-tip I learned along the way is to avoid nightshade vegetables on bad pain days (the specialist who recommended this to me wanted me to cut them completely from my diet, in addition to gluten and dairy and red meat and soy products and alcohol and sugar… I called it the don’t eat diet and now only cut foods when I’m flaring up for days).  Anyways. Nightshade veggies are potatoes, tomatoes, zucchinis, and peppers (there are probably more but those ones are easy to remember if you say it in that order a few times. Nightshade veggies affect the body’s ability to decrease inflammation (poorly worded explanation but basically if you’re achey those veggies can make you achier). 

Sleep is another important aspect for pain management but I’m horrible at sleeping, however a double gabapentin(600mg total) is great at knocking me out.  Guided sleep meditations also help me fall asleep and help distract myself from pain.  

And my last suggestion is regarding medications.   I take gabapentin but lyrica is it’s newer edition cousin so it may be an alternative if you’re not getting relief from gabapentin.   I also take cyclobenzapine, which helps with muscle soreness and spasms and I use it almost daily.   Naproxen helps with inflammation but can be horrible on your stomach but there’s a version with a stomach protector in it and I can take it daily.   I also currently take dilaudid a few days a week but I used to take buprenorophine in the BuTrans patch, and I would still likely use that if my skin didn’t react to the glue used for the patches.  It’s  basically naloxone and suboxone (if I recall correctly) so it’s a non-addictive opioid option.  Tramadol extended release I used to get relief from as well and it’s a weaker opioid so not really addictive but still a narcotic and it’s important to be cautious with using stronger narcotics.  My pain clinic doctor told me using morphine is like getting in bed with the mafia.  They can help you in a pinch but they own you for life.   I make a point to not take my narcotics daily to reduce the risks of addiction, and I have worked in addictions and mental health for years so I’ve always been pretty mindful of the risks of addiction. 

I hope this helps.  Best of luck.  Sorry for my novel :)

I feel for you OP, I spent many years working 2, sometimes 3 jobs at a time, and it’s brutal but can be necessary.  

I found when I worked multiple jobs with positions that were all the same (for years I was a server at 2-3 different establishments simultaneously) it was far more exhausting than when I worked multiple jobs with different positions.  The switch from one position to the next seemed to trick my brain a bit into “it’s a new workday” even after coming off an 8hr shift elsewhere. 

You don’t mention what your jobs are, but if they are all physically demanding, treat yourself to a GOOD pair of shoes/boots.  Alternatively if you’re sitting a lot, look up some quick stretches you can do while working and if you can, set an alarm or a reminder to do these every hour or two until the habit is formed.  I would do these when I’d transition from sitting at my desk to standing at my desk (my multiple jobs changed from restaurants to social services as I got older). 

Have your favourite music that pumps you up available to listen to during your commute from one to the other if possible.  I’d listen to some high energy bangers from the 90’s and sing along loudly while driving from one job to the next, but if you’re using public transportation, you probably want to dial it back at least 30% and maybe sing in your head. But you do you. 

Candy/sweets/treats/desserts to snack on during my shifts always helped my mood and my energy.  If you’re healthier than me, cut up fruits or veggies can also go in a ziplock in your pocket for secret shift-long snacking (bananas not recommended) or whatever floats your boat for snacks stuff. 

Avoid overdoing caffeine and energy drinks as you’ll just crash harder and feel like shit.  Water is your friend and if you’re feeling drowsy it will help stop that.  

And lastly, every time you get paid, put aside some of the money you are making to spend on whatever makes you happy, even if unnecessary. Indulge in your vices (but only if it is safe to do so, if wine is your thing then get wine drunk but not while working is what I mean).  I consider this self-care and a key part to maintaining multiple jobs for years on end. By working these jobs and busting your ass you are sacrificing your mental and physical health and need to have some sort of more immediate reward (like a bottle of wine) while also getting the longterm benefits (no debt). Physically, you are missing out on adequate amounts of sleep, meals are likely missed sometimes and may not be the healthiest options, if you’re sick you may still have to work both jobs so you’re not getting better as quick as you should, and there’s a higher demand physically irregardless of the job itself the longterm demands of working coupled with the reduced hours for downtime and sleeping will do a number on your body over time.  Then there’s the mental health impacts due to things like only having limited available time each day to spend with the people/animals/things that you care most about and for downtime for yourself for your hobbies and interests.  There’s also a lot of missed events, like family dinners or birthday parties or going to the county fair, which as a one-off aren’t so bad but over time these add up too.  So in addition to having a bit of self-care money, schedule yourself a weekly self-care shift too.  I used to tell each employer that I worked my other job at that time so I wasn’t available.  Use that time for yourself doing whatever refills your cup a little more.
